instance: adversarial-loop.js's defaultFindingKey keyed dedup identity on `location|category`; the same defect flagged by the security, spec-violation, and edges lenses got three different keys because each lens used a different category, so duplicates never collapsed. First run against 3 planted defects reported confirmed_count:12 and ran to the round cap (~1M tokens) instead of terminating dry.
check: Assert dedup collapses a cross-lens duplicate finding reported under different lens categories to one confirmed entry.

instance: adversarial-loop.js's verify threshold defaulted to Math.ceil(verifyVotes/2), which equals 1 for the default of 2 votes, so a single non-refuting skeptic could confirm a finding; a near-clean run confirmed a weak finding on a 1-of-2 vote.
check: Verify gate requires floor(n/2)+1 (strict majority), not ceil(n/2); test that a 1-of-2 vote does not confirm.

instance: The adversarial-clean validation run assumed a 3-line `clamp` fixture was defect-free and expected 0 confirmed findings; real attackers found a genuine NaN-boundary bug (NaN defeats the lo>hi guard because every NaN comparison is false), so the 'known-good' fixture was not actually clean.
check: Judge the discovery loop by termination behavior (goes dry, bounded, ranks correctly), never by whether a 'clean' fixture yields a specific finding count.

instance: The original cross-lens dedup unit test used the SAME category label for both simulated lenses, so it passed even though the real code (which keyed dedup on category) was broken — the mock fixture encoded the implementer's assumption instead of modeling that real lenses assign different categories to the same defect.
check: Mock/stub fixtures for a fan-out must mirror real diversity: different categories, location formats, and phrasings for the same underlying defect.

instance: cli-dispatch start (the mandated cross-model review channel) fetches origin first and exits 128 when a repo has no remote, but `start` is documented to exit 0 even on failure — a naive `start && next` chain on a greenfield repo would treat the no-op as success.
check: Parse cli-dispatch's structured status output rather than chaining on exit code alone; test start against a repo with no remote.

instance: adversarial-loop.js's dry-streak termination logic reset the streak whenever a round produced any fresh (unseen) finding key, so an attacker emitting novel-but-wrong claims every round kept the streak from accruing, running the loop to the round cap and paying full fan-out cost each round.
check: Define 'dry' on confirmed progress (K rounds with no new CONFIRMED defect), not on raw claim novelty; test with an attacker emitting endless novel-but-false claims.

instance: creation-loop.js's QA gate used `if (!verdict || verdict.ran_ok === false) escalate`, so a verdict with `passed:true` and no `ran_ok` field at all (schema not enforced, or a looser custom schema) fell through to the pass branch — a green-looking result that never actually asserted it ran.
check: Fail-closed gate must treat everything that is not an explicit consistent success as failure: `ran_ok !== true` escalates, `passed !== true` fails, and `passed:true` with listed failures is contradictory and fails.

instance: creation-loop.js's IMPLEMENT step returned `file_path` but the loop discarded it before QA, so QA received only the acceptance criteria (not the concrete artifact locator) — QA could write a green suite against the wrong path, a stale version, or invented helpers and still report ran_ok=true, passed=true.
check: Thread the concrete artifact locator (path + a cheap identity signal) into the QA gate and require QA to report what it actually tested, so a mismatch can be structurally rejected.

instance: defaultFindingKey's location-only dedup key over-merges two distinct defects sharing one line, and suffers 'reject-poison': a rejected claim's key enters `seen` before verification, so it can block a later correct claim at the same line.
check: Document lossy dedup explicitly as a false-negative risk (not just 'residual double-counting'); provide an optional fingerprint/keyOf escape hatch.

instance: For aifleet issue #590 (validate-fleet.sh's /registry check failing intermittently in CI), the coordinator's task assumed a transient network flake and had QA build a mock-server reproduction of that hypothesis; QA's test passed cleanly (ran_ok=true, passed=true, 0 replans) and the retry-loop PR landed, but CI failed again with the same symptom ~5s later — the real cause was the controller pod silently losing its K8s API connection (HTTP 500, stale route after 15 days uptime), unrelated to network timing, which the retry loop could not fix.
check: Before writing a Creation Loop task for a live, already-occurring failure, reproduce the failure directly against the real system first (actual exit code/HTTP status/log line) and put that confirmed reproduction in the task prompt itself.

instance: In Phase D's Adversarial smoke test (smoke-adversarial-worktree.js) against one planted off-by-one defect at paginate.js:5, codex and grok independently invented 4 different free-text fingerprints for the same bug; the FM-9 fingerprint escape hatch let these differing tags split what should have collapsed, so the loop reported confirmed_count:5 for one real defect (a 4x overcount) and dryStreak never advanced because each restated claim looked novel.
check: Test that an anchor (file:line) is authoritative and collapses all findings at that location regardless of fingerprint wording; test that fingerprint may still disambiguate two genuinely distinct anchor-less findings.

instance: Every failure mode in this registry was found by running the orchestration code against a real or injected fault, not by inspecting it; FM-1 and FM-2 were both live in code that had already passed its first unit-test suite, and that suite was only extended to cover them after a real run exposed them.
check: Treat a green happy-path run as necessary but never sufficient; build the fault-injection path before trusting a suite.

instance: A trust/allowlist check matched the string `github.com[:/]owner/repo` anywhere in a URL instead of parsing the host — an attacker-controlled host embedding the trusted string in its path (https://evil.example/github.com/petersimmons1972/x.git) or userinfo (https://github.com@evil.com/...) was wrongly trusted, enabling RCE/privilege escalation. Codex reproduced it live (PR #19, wrote a PWNED file); Codex and grok-4.5 independently reproduced the same substring bug plus a related ssh-port parse bug (ssh://...:22/owner parsed owner as '22').
check: Adversarial test placing the trusted substring in the path and userinfo of an untrusted host, plus a legit-URL table (https, ssh, ssh+port, scp-style).

instance: Round-1 PRs #19 and #20 both shipped green test suites written by the fixer, but each missed a blocker that an independent adversarial reviewer then found via a proof-of-concept — the tests confirmed the fix rather than trying to defeat it.
check: For every fix, write at least one test that actively tries to break it; require independent adversarial review by a different engine, ideally with a PoC.

instance: PR #20 changed a predicate from `conclusion == "SUCCESS"` to `conclusion != "SUCCESS"` in evaluate_checks, silently broadening the matched set to also count NEUTRAL/SKIPPED as failures and refuse healthy PRs; docs still described the old set and no test covered the newly-included values.
check: Enumerate every value newly included/excluded when touching a filter/predicate; test the newly-affected values; check doc-vs-code consistency.

instance: cli-dispatch issues #13/#17/#11 involved honoring untrusted control input as authoritative: run/cwd read from a repo's checked-in config, deleting a branch named in a harness-writable meta.json, and treating a VERDICT:/approval from any unauthenticated PR commenter as valid.
check: Adversarial test supplying hostile control input from each channel; gate executable config on origin ownership cross-checked against `git worktree list --porcelain`; verify commenter identity/allowlist, not just keyword presence.

instance: cli-dispatch #10: a command printed a failure status in its JSON output but still exited 0, so a naive `cmd && next` chain proceeded past a failed run because only the output channel encoded failure, not the exit status.
check: Test asserting the exit code (not just output text) for each terminal state.

instance: engram-go PR #1405 round 1: a review instruction told the implementer to apply distinct-dated-occurrence dedup to both `event` and `status_change` atoms; the implementer complied literally and broke status-supersession, since a repeated status_change is reinforcement of a transition, not a new occurrence.
check: Adversarial re-check per type in round 2: does the invariant this fix enforces actually hold for this type?

instance: engram-go PR #1405: a dedup fix was verified call-to-call across ingest passes but not within one candidate batch; a concurrent windowing change in the same PR raised per-call candidate cardinality through the same chokepoint and reintroduced the same data loss in-batch, caught only in round 3 of review.
check: Same-batch adversarial test with cardinality > 1 through the chokepoint, re-run whenever a PR touches batch/window sizing near a known chokepoint.

instance: A GB10 decode benchmark computed effective memory bandwidth as decode_tok/s x bytes_per_token using ollama /api/ps's resident_bytes (total VRAM footprint including KV cache at num_ctx=40960 and compute buffers) as bytes-read-per-token, producing 269-744 GB/s -- up to 2.7x the 273 GB/s hardware ceiling, a physically impossible result.
check: Sanity-bound every derived ratio against its theoretical ceiling before reporting; a ratio exceeding 1.0 or varying wildly is a denominator bug, not a discovery.

instance: A GB10 benchmark campaign gated every model load with an arithmetic canary ('17+18'='35') meant to catch corrupt/degenerate output; a 0.5B model and qwen3 thinking-mode models failed this canary for benign reasons (too small to compute it; reasoning tokens pushed '35' past the token window) even though their throughput data was valid, conflating output correctness/capability with output corruption.
check: Before adopting a canary, ask whether a valid healthy subject could fail it for a reason unrelated to the guarded fault; for corruption detection assert non-degenerate output rather than a capability task.

instance: A GB10 quality x speed benchmark reused num_predict=256 (tuned for throughput measurement) to grade answer accuracy of qwen3:8b (thinking-mode); the model spent the whole budget inside <think> and never emitted an answer, scoring as degenerate/incorrect -- and this hit FP16 more often than Q4/Q8 (FP16 reasoned longer), making the highest-fidelity quant falsely appear least accurate.
check: Treat an inverted fidelity/accuracy ordering (most-capable config scoring worst) as a measurement-artifact alarm; branch corruption checks on done_reason=='length' with empty answer (exclude as budget artifact) vs all-garbage output (fail as corrupt).

instance: An eval task (harness/corpus/taskSFA_typed.py, SF-A S1 typed-slot probe) certified uniqueness of a withheld rule by having the generator exhaustively enumerate the entire candidate space and refute every non-match; a zero-induction actor running the identical enumeration over prompt-visible constraints alone scored 40/40 at k=4/k=5 (plus correct at k=6/k=7) with no model spend, since the certificate's exhaustiveness proof IS the actor's search program, and the actor's enumeration was ~150x cheaper than the generator's certification (~16us vs ~2.4ms per inhabitant at k=7, |C|=5040).
check: Before trusting an enumeration-based uniqueness certificate as evidence a task requires induction, build a zero-induction falsifier (a solver using only prompt-visible material) and run it; if it scores comparably to a genuine actor, the certificate was never evidence against search.

instance: In the GB10 campaign, hand-authored 'quick/throwaway' benchmark harness scripts (campaign 1) later FAILED the repo's shellcheck CI gate, while campaign 2's harnesses -- authored via cli-dispatch/Codex under the fleet-standards floor -- passed shellcheck/ruff/bash-n clean on first submission, because skipping the standards-enforcing channel for 'quick' code reintroduced exactly the lint debt the floor exists to prevent.
check: If your own hand-authored code fails a gate your delegated code passes, that disproves the 'too small to bother' exemption; treat any un-delegated code as unverified until run through the same lint/gate.

instance: A GB10 S1 context x concurrency serving benchmark ran max_tokens=64 against prompts up to 32k tokens; the headline aggregate_tok_s metric stayed flat (~5.7-5.95 tok/s) across concurrency 1/4/16/32/64 at 32k context despite per-stream decode rate varying ~18x (40.3->2.18 tok/s) and TTFT varying ~37x (9.6s->353.6s), because wall-clock was dominated by prefill/TTFT rather than decode with such a short generation window.
check: Before trusting an aggregate tokens/wall_s number as decode capacity, check whether decode time actually dominates wall-clock at the longest context/highest concurrency cell; a flat aggregate against a variable expected to move it, while a component metric swings widely, is the alarm.

instance: A GB10 L1 prefill-vs-length scaling sweep built prompts by repeating a fixed paragraph to reach N tokens, making build_prompt(64000) a literal token-prefix of build_prompt(90000); run ascending inside one server session with --enable-prefix-caching on, the largest target's tokens were mostly already resident in cache from the preceding smaller target, inflating the reported prefill rate and making the curve read as flattening/improving. An isolated single-target rerun at 108,976 tokens measured TTFT 38.64s/2820 tok/s vs 14.76s/7382 tok/s inside the ascending sweep -- 2.62x slower isolated.
check: For a cold prefill-vs-length sweep, disable prefix caching or give each target a unique leading nonce so no build_prompt(N) is a prefix of build_prompt(M>N); verify by spot-checking one point in isolation against the full sweep.

instance: A GB10 Q2 quantization-quality-knee experiment for qwen3:8b was designed to sweep a full 7-point quant ladder, but 4 of 7 quant tags (q6_K, q5_K_M, q3_K_M, q2_K) pull_failed at run time because those tags don't exist in ollama's registry for this model -- only fp16/q8_0/q4_K_M do -- and the experiment's target sub-q4 knee region fell entirely inside the missing tags, so the knee went unmeasured despite the run completing 'successfully' via fail-open.
check: Verify tag availability against the target registry (or a live pull probe) for every planned sweep cell before designing the sweep; log a per-cell canary_ok/pull_failed field so silent gaps are visible in the data.

instance: A GB10 Q2 tiered (easy/medium/hard) quality eval used one fixed num_predict=1024 budget for a thinking-mode model across all tiers; the hard tier (the one the experiment was designed to discriminate on) got truncated and excluded far more than easy: fp16 scored only 12/20 hard items and 16/20 medium vs 19/20 easy, so the hardest tier ended up with the thinnest evidence (n=12-13 vs planned 20) exactly where the clearest finding was reported.
check: Check per-tier n_scored/n_total before trusting a tiered result -- if the tier you care about most has the lowest completion rate, the finding on that tier is thin evidence dressed as a clean number.

instance: grok-4.5 was declared unable to 'code headless' after being invoked via the interactive TUI form (`grok "prompt"` -> /dev/tty ENXIO) and a nonexistent sandbox profile; the correct invocation (`grok -p ... --sandbox workspace --check` or `grok agent`) worked. The same anti-pattern recurred 2026-07-11 as a codex 'large-prompt wedge' that was actually a stdin-hang.
check: Smoke-probe a harness's actual capability with one trivial live task before fanning out and before concluding it lacks a capability; treat any 'model X can't do Y' note as suspect until re-probed.

instance: A background research subagent went quiet with no completion notification after ~6 hours and was declared dead and relaunched; the original was actually alive and slow (ran 7.4h total), so both copies kept running and the original's un-allowlisted search-tool calls hit the founder as permission prompts for hours.
check: Before relaunching a 'stuck' background agent, verify it is actually dead (process/transcript mtime check) and TaskStop it first if alive; confirm a subagent's tools are allowlisted before a long fan-out.

instance: An 8.5h atom-build job exited 0 having embedded 0 of 16,792 atoms because the embed URL silently defaulted to the --llm-url (a non-embedder), 404-ing on every call; a relaunched extraction again 'progressed' while storing 0, and a ledger arm ran clean but its ledger was empty -- exit 0/'DONE' was read as proof of success when it only proved the process ended.
check: Smoke-test any long/background run on a cheap 1-N-item subset and assert on the real output artifact (row count > 0, required field present, live round-trip fetch) -- not the exit code.

instance: The 'instinct' self-improving subsystem's mistral judge dependency 404'd for three consecutive weeks; the except/catch path returned a substantive domain verdict ('reject') for each error instead of an abstain, so false_positive_rate kept reporting 0 while the judge was actually unreachable the whole time.
check: Test that a dependency error yields ABSTAIN/UNKNOWN and halts-or-alarms the batch, never a valid domain value; alarm when abstain-rate spikes.

instance: The instinct subsystem's false_positive_rate metric read 0 identically whether the system was healthy, broken (judge 404ing), or the store was empty, for two months -- a total==0 guard collapsed all three states onto the same 'healthy-looking' value so the metric could never fire.
check: Write the health metric's value in three states (working/broken/idle) before shipping it; if any two match, it's decoration. Emit an explicit state enum and alarm on degraded/idle-when-busy-expected.

instance: The instinct subsystem's repetition/toil detector hashed `tool:args:timestamp` as its dedup key across 43,078 logged events, producing 43,078 distinct hashes with zero collisions -- the identity key included the timestamp (per-occurrence variable data), so repetition was structurally undetectable.
check: Hash a normalized signature stripping variable args/timestamps/volatile path segments; assert distinct_keys < total_rows on a real sample, or the dedup does nothing.

instance: The instinct self-observing subsystem's learned 'patterns' were mostly about its own activity rather than the system it was meant to watch, because the observer logged its own calls and instrumented the easy-to-log actuation layer instead of the decision layer; the memory system it fed was touched only ~204 times out of 43,078 events (~0.5%).
check: Filter the corpus by source and confirm the observer isn't the loudest subject; measure a recall->action-change counter, not a raw store/call counter.

instance: The original single growing coding-failure-mode registry mixed three lifecycles with incompatible needs (durable invariants, transient tool-invocation quirks, brief-writing checklist rules) into one file, so none of it was actionable and the tool-quirk entries never expired; it was split 2026-07-11 into CODING-INVARIANTS.md, fleet-ops-log/2026-Q3.md, and DISPATCH-BRIEF-CHECKLIST.md.
A previously-recorded 'per-lane prompt-size ceiling' finding (FM-C4) was retracted -- the underlying incident was actually a stdin-hang (FM-B5), not a genuine prompt-size limit.

source_anchor: CI-18 — A capability restriction enforced after the fact on a lane that was *provisioned with* the capability
instance: `cli-dispatch`'s `consult_only` harness restriction ("brief in, text out; never lands a branch") was implemented three times as checks over a lane that was still handed a writable git worktree, a ready-made `origin` remote, and the operator's inherited push credentials. Round 1 refused a flag combination at harness selection; a harness that committed on its own still pushed. Round 2 added four barriers plus a `land` guard; adversarial verification measured three ways past them — a `run` template that pushed **during** its own execution (every barrier ran only after the harness process exited), a `land` bypass by renaming the hand-pushed branch out of `dispatch/<task>` so the guard's `if managed` block never ran, and a `land` bypass by passing `--task` naming an unrelated record. Each barrier was real, tested, and individually correct; the count of them read as depth. treating a restriction as a *policy over behaviour* rather than a *property of the environment*. A check evaluated after the actor already holds the capability is a race the actor can win; a check evaluated before it is one the actor can reach around. The lane was built out of exactly the same materials as an unrestricted lane, and only the checks differed — so every check sat at a point that could be routed around, and every hardening round added another such point.
check: when a lane, role, or agent must never do X, remove what it is *given* that makes X possible before writing any check that forbids X. Here: no `git worktree add` (so no branch and no ref exists to rename, push, or land), a `git archive` **export** instead of a clone (no repository, no remote, nothing to push from), a `.git` barrier file so repository *discovery* cannot climb into the shared checkout — a filesystem object, not an env var the harness can unset — and an `env` prefix that strips the token variables, the askpass variables, the agent socket, and the global/system git config the credential helper lives in. Keep the old checks, restated as **invariant asserts** whose firing means your own bookkeeping is broken; never let them be the mechanism. test the **absence**, not the refusal — assert that no ref exists locally or on origin, that repository discovery from inside the lane fails without reaching the parent repo, that the credential variables are unset *in the child process* (measured by a probe harness that dumps its own environment), and that an identically-provisioned lane *without* the restriction still shows all of them. Then mutate the provisioning — delete the barrier file, no-op the credential scrub, restore the worktree — and confirm each absence test fails; a test that passes under the mutation was never measuring the property. Reviewer heuristic: "we added a fourth barrier" is evidence the first three were the wrong shape, not that the fourth is the right one.

source_anchor: CI-19 — A credential-scrub enumeration modeled only the channels that go through config files, and missed the one that doesn't
instance: the round-3 fix for CI-18 stripped every env var and config path `git`/`gh` actually read for push credentials, but a workstation's `gh` OAuth token can also live in the OS keyring (GNOME/KDE Secret Service), reachable by any same-user process via `secret-tool`/libsecret over the D-Bus session bus — a path that consults none of `GH_CONFIG_DIR`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, or any token env var. Measured on a real session: `secret-tool search service gh:github.com` returned the stored credential using only `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`. the enumeration was scoped to the target program's (git/gh) own documented config surface, not to everything a same-privilege process can reach on the host. A shared desktop session shares the D-Bus bus and keyring daemon regardless of what any one program's config says.
check: for a same-user credential scrub, enumerate IPC channels (D-Bus session bus, keyring/agent sockets) before enumerating the target program's config surface. Here: unset `DISPLAY`/`XAUTHORITY` (denies X11 autolaunch) and `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`/`DBUS_STARTER_ADDRESS`/`DBUS_STARTER_BUS_TYPE` (denies direct address), and repoint `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` at an empty directory — the address-unset step alone is insufficient because the D-Bus spec's own fallback path is `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus`. a probe that reproduces the real client-library address-resolution order (direct address → runtime-dir fallback socket → X11 autolaunch), run inside the scrubbed environment, and a sibling probe confirming an unscrubbed (build) lane still resolves it — the discriminating pair, not a single assertion.

source_anchor: ORC-21 — Invariant 6 was asserted in a comment and never resolved in the code
instance: `orchestration/src/adversarial-loop.js` — the header comment stated *"premise diversity is the core … vary the premise, not the reviewer"* while the fan-out called `configuredModel(model, 'attack')` inside `lenses.map((lens) => …)`. `configuredModel` takes `(configModel, role)`; `lens` is not a parameter and cannot influence the result. the call sits inside the per-lens `map`, so it *reads* as if it varies per lens. Only its arguments say otherwise. Five premise-diverse prompts, one provider — and the loop then reported their agreement (and the skeptics' unanimity) as verification. the gate is one-directional by construction — confirmed defects still fail, so it can only move pass -> fail. Mutation-checked: suppressing findings from a non-independent panel (the inverted fix) fails 15 tests including `'adversarial #192: the independence gate never turns a failure into a success'`. `orchestration/test/adversarial-loop.test.js` — the eight `adversarial #192:` cases, notably `'independence is by SERVING FAMILY, not by model alias or CLI brand'` (three anthropic aliases must read as ONE reviewer) and `'a CLEAN sweep by a single-family panel is not reported as pass'`.
check: actors resolve per SLOT (`model.attack` / `model.verify` accept an array or a per-lens map), independence is computed by SERVING FAMILY via `actor-registry.servingFamilyOf` (provider, not model alias, not CLI brand), the result carries an `independence` block and each finding carries `corroborated`/`voter_families`, and a clean sweep by a panel that is not attested-independent returns `verdict:'fail'` + `not_corroborated:true` instead of `'pass'`. Opting out is explicit (`requireIndependence:false`) and recorded (`independence.waived`).
